passage:
Baisakhi evening, and the whole lane smelled of fresh wheat.
"Manoj bhaiya, did you see the new man in the Gill house? He sits on the step reading all day. He wears glasses. He hardly talks."
"So?"
"So he's a librarian! Definitely."
"Hmm. How many librarians do you know in our village?"
Sahil thought. "Zero. There's one at the town library."
"And how many farmers?"
"Everyone. Papa, Chacha, Gill uncle, the whole lane."
"So a quiet man who likes books, in a village full of farmers. What's he more likely to be?"
"But he LOOKS like a librarian!"
"Farmers read too, you know. Papa reads the newspaper twice every morning."
Sahil frowned at the wheat stacks. "Okay. Maybe a farmer who likes books."
"Tomorrow, go and ask him."

qa.q: What does the new man in the Gill house do all day?
qa.a: He sits on the step reading all day.

qa.q: Why was Sahil so sure the man must be a librarian?
qa.a: The picture of a quiet man with glasses and books felt so right that Sahil felt certain and excited, forgetting how many more farmers there are.

qa.q: What question from Manoj bhaiya helped Sahil think again?
qa.a: Asking how many librarians and how many farmers Sahil knew in the village, which brought the numbers back into the guess.

qa.q: How might the new man feel if the lane guessed his job from his books?
qa.a: He might feel amused or a little misunderstood, being judged by his reading instead of simply being asked.

grounding: Shows a child deciding a quiet book-lover must be a librarian, forgetting how many more farmers there are around him.

passage:
"Nandini, it's confirmed. The maths board paper has leaked."
"Confirmed by who?"
"My cousin's friend's uncle works at the printing press. He saw the envelope open. He even said the paper was blue, with a crease on the second page."
"Kalyani, how many times has the board paper actually leaked?"
"Once? Years ago?"
"And how many times has someone said it leaked?"
Kalyani paused, twirling her dandiya stick; the Navratri music was already starting in the school ground. "Every year, I guess."
"So which is more likely: this is the one rare real leak, or the usual rumour with extra details?"
"But the crease! Nobody makes up a crease."
"People make up creases all the time."
"Fine. But I'm still skipping chapter nine."
"Then I'm revising it twice, just for you."

qa.q: Where does Kalyani say the uncle works?
qa.a: At the printing press.

qa.q: Why does Kalyani feel sure the paper leaked?
qa.a: The vivid details, like the blue paper and the crease, make the report feel reliable, so Kalyani feels convinced and excited, forgetting how rare real leaks are.

qa.q: What would you advise Kalyani about chapter nine?
qa.a: Keep revising it, since real leaks are rare while rumours come every year, and check any such news with a teacher.

qa.q: How does Nandini judge the rumour?
qa.a: Nandini compares how seldom real leaks happen with how often rumours appear every year, so the extra details don't impress her.

grounding: Shows a teenager sure a rare exam leak happened because a detailed report seemed reliable, ignoring how uncommon real leaks are.

passage:
[Holi break, 1:12 am]
Amandeep: u awake?
Gopika: ya whats up
Amandeep: the college health camp result came as an sms. my screening for that rare condition is positive
Amandeep: been reading online for 2 hours. i think i actually have it
Gopika: wait. what did the doctor say
Amandeep: haven't seen the doctor, just the sms
Gopika: ok. the leaflet from the camp said the condition itself is really rare na
Gopika: and that the screening flags lots of people who turn out fine. that's why there's a second test
Amandeep: but it SAYS positive
Gopika: positive means "check again", not "you have it". ask the camp doctor to explain tomorrow. i'll come with u
Amandeep: ok. still scared
Gopika: i know. stop reading, try to sleep. meet at 10 🤍

qa.q: How did Amandeep get the college health camp result?
qa.a: The college health camp result came as an sms.

qa.q: Why is Amandeep so sure of having the condition?
qa.a: The word "positive" feels final, so Amandeep feels frightened and panicky, forgetting how rare the condition is and how many screenings turn out to be false alarms.

qa.q: What is the wise next step for Amandeep?
qa.a: Stop reading online, try to sleep, and ask the camp doctor tomorrow to explain what the result means, with Gopika there for support.

qa.q: How does Gopika read the same result?
qa.a: Gopika sees "positive" as a reason to check again, remembering the leaflet said the condition is rare and the screening flags many people who are fine.

grounding: Shows a student fearing a rare condition after a positive screening result, not realising that most positives for rare conditions turn out to be false alarms.

passage: When the building's water report came back last August with "bacteria detected" in the third-floor sample, Kishore, our society secretary, wanted to shut off the supply to all forty flats that night. I asked for ten minutes. He sighed. "Fine, Tanuja. Ten." First I looked at the history: in four years of monthly tests, the building had one bad result, and that came from a dirty sample bottle. So a real problem was possible but not the likeliest story. Then I adjusted for what was different this time: the tank had been cleaned a week earlier, and two families on the third floor said the water smelled odd. That pushed my worry up. I called the lab and asked the technician to explain the result and whether a retest made sense. The advice was bottled water on the third floor and a retest next morning. The retest was clear; the smell came from a new pipe seal.

qa.q: How many bad results had the building had in four years of monthly tests?
qa.a: One bad result, which came from a dirty sample bottle.

qa.q: What did Tanuja feel when the two families mentioned the smell?
qa.a: Tanuja became more uneasy and alert, since that evidence made a real problem more likely than the history alone suggested.

qa.q: Which steps made Tanuja's reasoning careful?
qa.a: Starting with how rare bad results had been, adjusting for the cleaning and the smell, and asking the lab technician to explain before deciding.

qa.q: How did Kishore react to the report at first?
qa.a: Kishore was alarmed and wanted to shut off the supply to all forty flats that night.

grounding: Shows a careful thinker starting from how often bad results happen, adjusting for the specific evidence, and asking a professional to explain the result.

passage: During the winter carnival week, the school library was the only quiet place left. Salma and Deepa watched the new boy, Siddharth, sketching in a corner with his hood up. "Bet time," Deepa whispered. "Which is more likely: he's an artist, or he's a shy artist who secretly writes poems?" "The second one, obviously," Salma said. "Look at him. The hood, the silence, the little notebook. It's a whole story." Deepa grinned. "But every shy poet-artist is also an artist. So the first one has to be at least as likely." Salma opened her mouth, closed it, then shook her head. "It still feels more true." Siddharth looked up, noticed them staring, and went back to his sketch of the library windows.

qa.q: Where was Siddharth sketching?
qa.a: In a corner of the school library, with his hood up.

qa.q: Why does the detailed guess feel right to Salma?
qa.a: The hood, the silence and the notebook fit together into a whole story, so Salma feels confident and pleased that it is more true, even though each detail makes it less likely.

qa.q: How could Salma check a guess like this next time?
qa.a: Salma could ask whether the detailed version is just one part of the simple one; if it is, the simple one can never be less likely.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel noticing them staring?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel a little awkward and self-conscious, not knowing he has become the subject of a bet.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging that a quiet boy is more likely a shy artist who writes poems than simply an artist, because the extra details feel truer.

passage:
Two weeks before Diwali: At the college fest meeting, Eshaan pitched his stall plan with shining eyes. "We get the corner spot by the gate, the dance club performs right next to us, my cousin lends his fairy lights, the mehendi artist comes at six, and we sell out by eight." Everyone cheered. Afreen's plan, "sell painted diyas, cover costs", got polite nods.
Fest day: The corner spot went to the music society. The dance club moved to the auditorium. The fairy lights came, but the mehendi artist had a wedding. By eight they had sold a third of the stock.
The Monday after: Eshaan sat with Afreen in the empty classroom, counting leftover diyas into boxes. "Every piece sounded so real," he said. "It was five things that all had to go right," Afreen said, "and each one could fall."

qa.q: How much of the stock had they sold by eight?
qa.a: A third of the stock.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan's detailed plan feel so believable?
qa.a: Each vivid step made the story feel more real, so Eshaan felt excited and confident, not noticing that every added step was another thing that had to go right.

qa.q: How could Eshaan plan the next stall more wisely?
qa.a: He could list each thing that has to go right, ask how likely each one is, and keep a simple backup like Afreen's plan to cover costs.

qa.q: How did Afreen see the pitch?
qa.a: Afreen saw five things that all had to go right, while her own simpler, more realistic plan got only polite nods.

grounding: Shows a student finding a detailed success story more believable than a simple one, though each added detail was one more thing that had to go right.

passage:
Subject: Thoughts on yesterday's rollout pitch
Hi Manjula,
Before we sign, one small worry about the vendor's pitch. It was brilliant: approval from the state portal in week two, all 40 branches trained by week four, the old system switched off in week five, fully live in six weeks, and zero downtime. Everyone in the room was nodding, me included.
But when I wrote it out, it's really five separate things that each have to go right, in order. Even if each one is quite likely, the chance of all five working together is a lot lower than any one of them. The detail made it feel more certain, when it actually makes it less so.
Could we ask them for a plan B for the two riskiest steps, and a date range instead of one date?
Thanks,
Indu

qa.q: How many branches did the pitch say would be trained by week four?
qa.a: All 40 branches.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling during the pitch and afterwards?
qa.a: Indu was impressed and nodding in the room, but later felt uneasy when writing the steps out showed how many had to go right together.

qa.q: What does Indu suggest, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Asking the vendor for a plan B for the two riskiest steps and a date range, because five linked steps rarely all go perfectly.

qa.q: How might Manjula react to the email?
qa.a: Manjula may feel a little deflated after an exciting pitch, but also grateful that the risk was spotted before signing.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a persuasive pitch full of specific steps and reminding the team that each extra step lowers the chance of everything working together.

passage:
"Joseph, I've figured it out. It's the red shirt."
"What about it?"
"Every day I wear my red shirt, our team wins. Monday, red shirt, we won. Wednesday, red shirt, won. Friday, blue shirt, lost!"
"Farhan, on Friday Ayaan was away at his Nani's for Christmas."
"So?"
"Ayaan's our best bowler. On Monday and Wednesday he was here."
"But I was wearing red!"
"You also wear red on Sundays, when we don't even play."
"That's different." Farhan tugged at his collar. "I'm wearing it tomorrow anyway. Just in case."
"Wear whatever you like. I'm making sure Ayaan comes."

qa.q: What shirt was Farhan wearing on Friday?
qa.a: A blue shirt.

qa.q: Why does Farhan believe the red shirt makes the team win?
qa.a: The wins and the red shirt kept happening together, so it feels like a real link, and Farhan feels excited and sure of having found the secret 😄

qa.q: What could Farhan check to test the shirt idea?
qa.a: He could note who played and which shirt he wore for many matches, and see whether the wins follow Ayaan or the shirt.

qa.q: What does Joseph think really made the difference?
qa.a: Joseph thinks it was Ayaan, the best bowler, who played on the winning days and was away on Friday.

grounding: Shows a child deciding his red shirt causes his team's wins because the two happened together.

passage: Charu, before you beg your father for that tuition, listen to your Vinita bua. It's Sankranti; fly your kite after. When I was fifteen, I noticed that every girl who went to Sharma sir's tuition scored in the eighties. So I decided tuition made you clever. I cried until Dada agreed to pay, though money was tight that winter. I went for a whole year and scored sixty-eight. Same as before. Then I looked properly at who went there: girls whose mothers sat with them every evening, who had their own desks, who already loved maths. They would have scored well anywhere. My friend Lata never went, studied under the streetlight, and got eighty-four. It wasn't the tuition. It was everything else those girls had. So first tell me why you want it, hmm?

qa.q: What did young Vinita score after a year of tuition?
qa.a: Sixty-eight, the same as before.

qa.q: Why did young Vinita believe tuition made students clever?
qa.a: Seeing every tuition girl score in the eighties made the link feel obvious, so Vinita felt certain and desperate to join, missing what else those girls had.

qa.q: What choice in the story could young Vinita have made before crying for tuition?
qa.a: Vinita could have looked at who went there and what else they had, like help at home and their own desks, before deciding the tuition was the cause.

qa.q: What does Lata's result show inside the story?
qa.a: Lata never went to tuition yet scored eighty-four, showing that Lata's own effort mattered more than tuition itself.

grounding: Shows a teenager concluding that tuition causes high scores, missing that the students who took it had other advantages too.

passage: Trisha, don't judge the mugs. You know I never drank coffee, right? Then last month, in the middle of the December exams, I read this headline: "Coffee drinkers live longer." A big study, thousands of people. I thought, that's it, science has spoken. So now it's three mugs a day. My mother thinks I've joined a cult. I told her, "Mummy, it's research, I'm investing in my future." Then my roommate asked who these coffee drinkers even were. Maybe people who can afford a café every morning, who have time to sit, who walk there. Maybe people who get sick stop drinking coffee, so the drinkers look healthier. I said she was overthinking it. But now I'm looking at mug number three, and I'm not so sure. Anyway, that's Rehana's great health plan. Want some?

qa.q: What did the headline say?
qa.a: "Coffee drinkers live longer."

qa.q: Why did Rehana feel so sure coffee was the reason?
qa.a: A big study with thousands of people felt like science had spoken, so Rehana felt confident and pleased about investing in the future.

qa.q: What questions could Rehana ask before believing a headline like this?
qa.a: Who the coffee drinkers were, what else might explain the link, like money, time or health, and whether the direction could run the other way.

qa.q: How does the roommate see the headline?
qa.a: The roommate suspects hidden factors, like affording a café or sick people giving up coffee, rather than coffee itself.

grounding: Shows a student believing coffee causes long life after reading a headline, missing hidden third factors and a possibly reversed direction.
